parole.testo: Possibly a calque of German Angelrute or calque of Dutch hengelroede; equivalent to angle (“to fish”) + rod.

parole.significato: To make a loud, hollow, resonant sound.
parole.testo: Onomatopoeic, perhaps borrowed; compare German bummen, Dutch bommen (“to hum, buzz”). The sense "a period of economic growth" is generally taken to derive from the sense "a rapid expansion", although other origins have also been suggested.

parole.significato: The sound of a horse's shod hoof striking the ground.
parole.testo: Perhaps from German or Dutch kloppen (“to hit, knock”), from Middle Dutch cloppen (“to make a clopping sound”), of onomatopoeic origin. See also clap.

parole.significato: One of a Native American tribe from the Southeastern United States, also known as the Muscogee.
parole.testo: * As an English surname, from Creake in Norfolk, a variant of the noun crag (“steep rugged cliff”). * Also as an English surname, from the archaic noun cratch (“crib, manger”). * As a German surname, Americanized from Krieg (“war, warfare”), Krück, Kruck (see Krug (“jug”) and Krücke (“crutch”)), Kri

parole.significato: Next to last, second to last.
parole.testo: From fore- + last. In some instances of more recent use, perhaps also a calque of German vorletzte or Dutch voorlaatst.

parole.significato: An informal greeting roughly equivalent to how are you.
parole.testo: The phrase is a regular Early Modern English equivalent of how's it going (when neither progressive tenses nor do-support were obligatory). As such it could have survived through regional dialects. Nevertheless modern usage is likely a calque of German wie geht es, perhaps additionally also Dutch ho

parole.significato: A small coaster vessel, usually sloop-rigged, used in conveying passengers and goods, or as a tender to larger vessels…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Heu or Dutch gooi.

parole.significato: An outdoor festival and fair, originally in a German or Dutch-speaking country
parole.testo: From German Kirmes and Dutch kermis, both originally “church mass”, referring to a festival on the anniversary of the consecration of a church. See respective entries for more.

parole.significato: The wife of a landgrave, or a woman who rules over a landgraviate.
parole.testo: From German Landgräfin and Dutch landgravin, equivalent to landgrave + -ine.

parole.significato: A geographical area where some language is commonly spoken.
parole.testo: Calque of German Sprachraum, Sprachgebiet, and/or Dutch taalgebied.

parole.significato: A measure of weight formerly used in Germany, the Netherlands and some other parts of Europe, equivalent to half of the…
parole.testo: From German Loth (obsolete), Lot, later also from Dutch lood, both specific usages of the word for ‘lead’. Doublet of lead.
Borrowed from German Mops (“pug”), from Dutch mops.
From sour + stuff. Calque of German Sauerstoff (“oxygen”) and/or Dutch zuurstof (“oxygen”), both loose loan translations of French oxygène. See oxygen for more.

Probably a calque of German Donnerbüchse (“(archaic) blunderbuss; cannon”) (from Donner (“thunder”) + Büchse (“box; can; rifle”)), or its etymon Dutch donderbus (“blunderbuss”) (from donder (“thunder”) + bus (“box; container; (chiefly historical) type of early modern firearm”)).
